strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: retaining information beyond a transformer’s context window in partially observed offline RL. The memory-token interface provides a straightforward adaptation of existing sequence models.

T-Maze provides concrete positive results: RATE achieves 100% success through three segments, and RATE-7 achieves 99.3% at five segments versus 48.9% for DT-7 (Table 2). Curriculum and memory-corruption ablations help demonstrate that the model uses stored information.

Evaluation covers two memory tasks, four Atari games, and nine MuJoCo settings. The paper includes substantial Atari improvements, several useful ablations, hyperparameter tables, and a source-code link.
weaknesses: The methodological novelty is limited: RATE largely combines Decision Transformer, Transformer-XL caching, and existing RMT memory tokens. The memory-task experiments lack strong recurrent alternatives, such as LSTM/GRU policies and a Transformer-XL-only baseline trained under the same conditions. Consequently, superiority to truncated-context DT does not establish the value of this particular memory architecture.

The DT comparisons do not adequately isolate the contribution. In VizDoom, RATE receives episode prefixes containing the initial cue, whereas DT receives random subsequences (Section 4.2). T-Maze’s baseline context is also inconsistently described: Section 4.3 discusses DT processing K×S contexts, while Section 5.1 specifies K-length subsequences. These differences need controlled comparisons and clarification.

VizDoom has an unresolved information-channel issue. Section 4.1 says rewards are withheld because they reveal the target color, but Table 6 describes changing return-to-go inputs. Under the stated update rule, consecutive returns reveal immediate rewards and therefore provide an alternative to remembering the initial cue. A constant-return RATE variant is evaluated, but an equivalent DT comparison is missing.

The central training procedure is contradictory. Section 3 states that the recurrent memory subsequence is detached, then claims gradients propagate through that same subsequence into the preceding segment; Figure 2 also depicts cross-segment gradients. These operations are incompatible as written. The paper needs an explicit recurrence and gradient-truncation specification, including how Transformer-XL caching interacts with memory tokens.

The conventional benchmarks weakly isolate memory’s benefit. On Qbert, RATE without memory tokens already scores 12,300, compared with 13,518 for RATE and 2,215.8 for DT (Table 3), accounting for most of the reported improvement. MuJoCo additionally resets the target return each segment while using published baseline scores, without an ablation separating this inference heuristic from the architecture.

The claimed significant VizDoom improvement is insufficiently supported statistically: RATE obtains 16.46 ± 6.90 versus DT90’s 6.08 ± 1.62, with the uncertainties labeled standard errors (Table 1). The default evaluation uses only three training seeds, and no significance analysis establishes the claim.

Long-horizon retention remains limited even on T-Maze’s single initial cue: RATE-7 falls to 66.1% success at twelve segments. The reported 100% success at 100 segments requires repeatedly reusing the first segment’s memory rather than the normal recurrent updates. This distinction materially limits the evidence for robust long-term memory.
